content: Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for individuals living with HIV (PLHIV) due to the shared modes of transmission and overlapping geographic prevalence of both infections. However, PLHIV may not achieve adequate sero-protection after receiving the standard hepatitis B vaccine because of their compromised immune systems. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy of the hepatitis B vaccine in PLHIV compared to a placebo or no vaccine. To achieve this, six English-language databases were searched in July 2012, with updates conducted in June 2013 and August 2014. Additional sources, such as grey literature, conference proceedings, specialized websites, and expert consultations, were also utilized. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared the hepatitis B vaccine to placebo or no vaccine, specifically evaluating outcomes related to efficacy and safety. Two independent reviewers extracted data from eligible studies, including information on study design, participant characteristics, hepatitis B infection rates, hepatitis B-related morbidity and mortality, anti-HBs immunogenicity, and vaccine-related adverse effects. The data were analyzed qualitatively. Only one double-blind RCT met the inclusion criteria. This study, conducted in Spain, involved 26 participants who were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART). The trial lasted three years, with monthly follow-ups. The study reported an adequate humoral immune response to the hepatitis B vaccine at 12 months, with no local or systemic side effects observed in either the vaccine or placebo groups. However, the humoral response diminished when participants discontinued ART. The study's small sample size and its setting in a high-income country limit its generalizability to regions with the highest burden of hepatitis B and HIV co-infections. The authors concluded that the evidence from this single study is insufficient to make definitive recommendations regarding the use of the hepatitis B vaccine in PLHIV. The study also does not provide evidence to suggest that the vaccine is unsafe in this population. Further RCTs conducted in high-prevalence areas are necessary to evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine in PLHIV, both with and without ART. Additionally, research should explore different vaccine regimens and routes of administration.
